doc.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Marriage, Chicago and arriving in New York
title: Jimmy turns down Condon's offer and they go to Chicago
summary: Eddie Condon offered Jimmy Wild Bill Davison's chair but Jimmy wanted to rest; she wonders how life would have differed, and notes Jimmy's constant support.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Was that with the same group of musicians, Wild Bill and that group you were playing with?
Yeah, but they were all somewhere else. They were probably downstairs imbibing and telling rude stories. Boy, when I think of all those guys.
O.k. That’s after you’d moved to New York at that point.
We hadn’t moved. We’d just arrived. It was like . . .

Actually at that time Condon asked Jimmy if—Wild Bill was leaving—asked Jimmy if he would like to join the band. I said, “My God, wonderful, why didn’t . . .” Jimmy refused utterly. “No, I want to go back to Chicago. I just got out of the army. I’ve just come back from Europe, and I want to see my family. I want to

relax. I don’t want to work.” I often think if he had taken that gig, I wonder how differently our lives would have been, or what I would have done, whether I would have done the same as I did if he had done that instead of us working together. Because I must say that Jimmy was always very supportive of me and probably more proud of what I was doing than he should have been. He accepted me for . . . He never pointed out any mistakes, “You shouldn’t play that chord.” He was very supportive. But I was still playing . . . I would play all the tunes, but when it was time for my feature, to do a number, I would do something ridiculous, like “Claire de lune.” The first date that we had in Chicago . . . We didn’t work for a while. We went out and lived with his sister and her family. We stayed there for a while.
